concepts.title: Scalar
concepts.mechanism: The important distinction is one value versus a collection of values. A scalar can record a temperature, a count, or a prediction error. Its numerical type does not tell us what it measures: the meaning and units come from the problem.
concepts.workedSteps: A second reading might be 25.0 °C. Subtracting the first numerical value from the second gives a rise of 0.5 °C: two scalar inputs produce one scalar difference. Keeping both readings is a collection, rather than a single scalar. Later, a learning algorithm will also use a scalar to summarize how badly its predictions missed their targets.

concepts.title: Variable
concepts.mechanism: Symbols let us state one relationship and reuse it for many cases. Keep track of the role of each symbol: some values are supplied, some are calculated, and some are quantities we want to find. Changing a symbol's value does not change the rule that uses it.
concepts.workedSteps: Read the calculation as a small process: take the input 3, double it to get 6, then add the fixed 1. The resulting 7 belongs to y. If the input changes, substitute the new value everywhere x occurs. This is how a single formula can describe many measurements or predictions without rewriting the calculation each time.

concepts.title: Function
concepts.mechanism: A function separates a reusable rule from the particular input passed to it. This is the basic shape of a prediction system: receive an allowed input, apply a rule, return an output. Knowing the output need not reveal the original input, because a function can discard information.
concepts.workedSteps: The rule squares its input. Starting with 3 or with −3 therefore reaches the same 9. The rule is perfectly definite in the forward direction, yet “which input produced 9?” has two answers here. This distinction matters whenever we transform measurements: an easy forward calculation may be impossible to undo uniquely.

concepts.title: Units
concepts.mechanism: Units help check whether an operation means what we think it means. Convert compatible measurements to a common unit before adding or comparing them. A computer can calculate with mismatched units without noticing; the result can still be meaningless.
concepts.workedSteps: Think of four one-second intervals. Each contributes 3 metres, so four such intervals contribute 12 metres in total. The same speed is 300 centimetres per second; multiplying by 4 gives 1,200 centimetres, the same distance. A changed numerical representation should not change the physical prediction.

concepts.title: Vector
concepts.mechanism: The order gives the numbers their roles. A vector might hold horizontal and vertical displacement, or two measurements of one object. Operations on vectors only make sense when the corresponding positions refer to compatible quantities. This is how a model can process several inputs together while keeping their identities.
concepts.workedSteps: For a displacement, start at the origin, move 2 units horizontally and 3 vertically. Doubling the vector doubles both movements, producing the same direction with twice the length. If instead the entries mean temperature and pressure, scaling still works coordinate by coordinate, but the geometric interpretation requires care because the units differ.

concepts.title: Matrix
concepts.mechanism: A matrix can organize many vectors: for example, one observation per row and one measured feature per column. Those meanings are part of the data specification. A matrix can also hold the coefficients of a transformation, which we will apply using matrix multiplication.
concepts.workedSteps: Suppose the first row describes observation A and the second describes observation B. Then the first feature is the column containing 1 and 4; the third feature is the column containing 3 and 6. Reading entry 6 means selecting observation B's third feature. Swapping rows changes observation order; swapping columns changes which measurement occupies each position.

concepts.title: Tensor
concepts.mechanism: Extra axes preserve structure that a single long list would hide. For example, several observations can each contain a table of measurements. The tensor stores all of them together, but an axis has no built-in meaning: its name and ordering must be specified before indexing or combining the data.
concepts.workedSteps: To find the displayed 6, first choose table 2, then its first row, then that row's second entry. Changing only the first index selects another table while keeping the same row and column. Flattening the stack into a list would keep its numbers, but recovering the table structure would also require remembering the original shape and ordering.

concepts.title: Summation
concepts.mechanism: The index is a bookkeeping device: expand the terms it names, then add each exactly once. Dividing a sum by the number of terms produces their arithmetic mean. Learning algorithms repeatedly use this pattern to combine contributions from many observations.
concepts.workedSteps: The three contributions are 2, 4, and 6; none is a multiplier or an extra index value. Their total is 12. Sharing that total equally across three positions gives the mean 4. A sum answers “how much altogether?” while a mean answers “how much per observation?” Doubling a dataset changes the sum but not its mean when all observations are duplicated.

concepts.title: Dot product
concepts.mechanism: A dot product is a weighted total: each weight determines how much the matching input contributes. Positive weights add in the same direction, negative weights subtract, and zero weights ignore an input. This operation will be the core calculation inside a simple artificial neuron.
concepts.workedSteps: Imagine two products with quantities 2 and 3 and unit prices 4 and 5. Their costs are 8 and 15, totaling 23. Pairing a quantity with the wrong price would change the meaning. The same arithmetic can combine measured features into a score; learning will later mean adjusting those weights from examples.

concepts.title: Matrix multiplication
concepts.mechanism: Matrix multiplication bundles many dot products into one operation. Each row of the left matrix supplies a different set of weights; each column of the right matrix supplies an input. The shared inner dimension ensures that each weight has one matching input value.
concepts.workedSteps: The column holds one input with two coordinates. The first row combines it with weights 1 and 2; the second uses weights 3 and 4. That produces two different output coordinates, 17 and 39, from the same input. Adding another input column would calculate both outputs for that input as well, without changing the transformation.

concepts.title: Transpose
concepts.mechanism: Transpose changes which index plays which role; it does not change the entries themselves. It is useful when a calculation needs observations arranged as columns instead of rows, or when we need to pair rows of one matrix with rows of another through a dot product.
concepts.workedSteps: All three numbers survive, in the same order, but the horizontal row becomes a vertical column. Transposing again restores the original row. No stretching has been undone and no equation has been solved: rearranging entries is different from finding an inverse transformation.

concepts.title: Linear transformation
concepts.mechanism: A matrix's columns show where the unit coordinate directions go. Any input can be built from those directions, so the transformation applies the same combination to their transformed versions. This lets a few coefficients describe the action on infinitely many possible inputs.
concepts.workedSteps: The horizontal unit direction becomes twice as long and the vertical one three times as long. The input contains one horizontal unit and two vertical units, so the result contains 2 horizontal units and 6 vertical units. The transformation changes the entire drawing consistently; it is not a separate rule invented for each point.

concepts.title: Euclidean distance
concepts.mechanism: Distance converts several coordinate differences into one measure of separation. Squaring prevents positive and negative differences from cancelling, and the square root returns the result to the coordinates' units. This can help find nearby observations, provided the coordinates' scales are meaningful.
concepts.workedSteps: Moving from the first point to the second changes the horizontal coordinate by 3 and the vertical by 4. These are perpendicular sides of a right triangle; the straight path is its hypotenuse, of length 5, not the 7-unit route along both sides. A feature measured on a much larger numerical scale can dominate this distance, even when it is not more important.

concepts.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
concepts.mechanism: Most vectors mix directions under a transformation. Eigenvectors reveal special directions whose behavior is simpler: repeated applications keep the vector on one line and repeatedly multiply its scale. They help explain which patterns grow, shrink, or reverse in a repeated process.
concepts.workedSteps: A vector with both coordinates nonzero usually changes its direction here because its horizontal part is multiplied by 2 while its vertical part is multiplied by 3. The coordinate arrows avoid that mixing. Repeating the transformation favors the vertical component because it grows by the larger factor on every application; this explains why the special directions are useful, beyond just naming them.

concepts.title: Singular value decomposition
concepts.mechanism: SVD separates the choice of directions from the amount of stretching. Keeping only the largest stretches gives a simpler approximation when the omitted directions contribute little to the task. It is used to compress a transformation and to expose directions that nearly disappear; a small stretch is not automatically unimportant to every task.
concepts.workedSteps: The compressed matrix needs only one input coordinate to reproduce its output, because the vertical contribution has been removed. For the displayed point, the missing vertical output is exactly the information lost. With a non-diagonal matrix, SVD first finds suitable perpendicular directions rather than assuming they are horizontal and vertical. Compression means choosing what to lose, not preserving every number for free.

concepts.title: Probability
concepts.mechanism: Start by specifying the possible outcomes and what event counts as success. Adding the probabilities of the outcomes in that event gives its probability. Counting outcomes works directly only when they are equally likely; otherwise their different weights must be respected.
concepts.workedSteps: The event “even” collects three die faces, while the full experiment has six equally likely faces. The fraction one-half describes that event before a throw. It does not say which particular face will occur, or promise an exact split in a short run. This distinction lets a predictive model express uncertainty instead of pretending every future outcome is determined.

concepts.title: Conditional probability
concepts.mechanism: Conditioning changes the group over which we count. First restrict attention to cases satisfying the information after “given”; then measure the requested event inside that group. It is useful when a prediction should change after part of an observation becomes known.
concepts.workedSteps: Once “red” is known, non-red balls are outside the relevant group. The denominator is four red balls, and the numerator is the one ball that is both red and striped. To reverse the question and ask about red balls among striped balls, we would need the total number of striped balls instead. The two denominators answer different questions.

concepts.title: Bayes’ theorem
concepts.mechanism: The update compares how well competing possibilities explain the evidence while retaining how common they were to begin with. Strong evidence can change a belief substantially, but an imperfect signal does not erase the base rate. This is useful for interpreting noisy alerts and updating predictions as evidence arrives.
concepts.workedSteps: Begin with the 10 defective and 90 good parts, then follow each group through the flagging process. Eight of the defects are flagged, but so are nine good parts. The alert therefore narrows attention to 17 parts, not just the eight true defects. Its usefulness comes from increasing the defect fraction above the original 10%, while leaving substantial uncertainty.

concepts.title: Expected value
concepts.mechanism: An expected value combines the magnitude of each outcome with how often it occurs. It is useful for comparing average consequences across repeated uncertain situations. It does not describe the spread of outcomes, and it need not be an outcome that can occur on any single trial.
concepts.workedSteps: Half of many trials contribute zero and half contribute ten on average, so the average payout approaches five under independent repetition. A single trial still pays only zero or ten. A guaranteed payout of five would have the same mean but a very different experience: uncertainty about individual outcomes has not vanished just because we summarized them by one number.

concepts.title: Variance
concepts.mechanism: The mean gives a center; variance asks how far values typically scatter around that center. Squaring makes both directions contribute positively and gives larger deviations more influence. Standard deviation expresses that spread back in the original measurement units.
concepts.workedSteps: Subtracting the mean 4 produces deviations −2 and 2. Their signed average is zero, even though the readings differ. Squaring makes both contributions 4, and averaging gives variance 4. The standard deviation 2 describes the spread around the mean; it is not an uncertainty bound guaranteeing that future readings stay inside a fixed interval.

concepts.title: Covariance and correlation
concepts.mechanism: Centering removes the two baseline levels before comparing their movement. Products of deviations are positive when both are above or both below their means, and negative when they move in opposite directions. Dividing by the two spreads makes correlation comparable across different measurement units.
concepts.workedSteps: The first observation is below both means and the second above both, so both products contribute positively. The perfect correlation describes the straight-line pattern in these two points, not evidence that one measurement causes the other. With only two distinct pairs, this apparent perfection is especially weak evidence about what a larger dataset will do.

concepts.title: Monte Carlo estimation
concepts.mechanism: A simulation replaces an expectation that is difficult to calculate directly with repeated experiments we can carry out. Each draw must follow the intended probabilities; compute the quantity of interest for that draw, then average. The approximation improves through sampling, not through finding a single “typical” outcome.
concepts.workedSteps: Keep a running total: after the four draws it reaches 12, which divided by four gives 3. Another set of four draws can give a different average. In the editable example, the simulated population is explicitly the four equally likely reward values, so its exact mean is available as a check. In larger problems, that exact comparison may be unavailable.

concepts.title: Exponential and logarithm
concepts.mechanism: Exponentials turn repeated multiplication into a function of the repetition count. Logarithms reverse that viewpoint and turn products into sums. This makes them useful both for growth processes and for handling probabilities whose products become extremely small.
concepts.workedSteps: Starting from one, three doublings produce two, four, then eight. The base-2 logarithm asks how many doublings connect one to eight. Natural logarithms use a different base but the same inverse idea. A logarithm reports a multiplicative change on an additive scale; it is not another name for division.

concepts.title: Derivative
concepts.mechanism: A derivative predicts the effect of a small input change near the current point. It gives local sensitivity, not the total change over an arbitrary interval. This is the information a training algorithm needs when deciding how to adjust a parameter to reduce an error.
concepts.workedSteps: The slope 6 predicts a change of about 0.06 for an input increase of 0.01. The actual change, 0.0601, is close but not identical because the curve bends over that interval. The tangent in the plot represents this local straight-line prediction. Move the input and both its slope and the point of contact change.

concepts.title: Integral
concepts.mechanism: Integration combines local contributions into a total. Split the interval into pieces, multiply each rate by its piece's duration, and add; smaller pieces allow a changing rate to be represented more faithfully. It connects a description of “how fast” with one of “how much.”
concepts.workedSteps: During each of the three seconds, two litres enter the tank. Adding those contributions produces six litres. For a varying flow, rectangles with different heights approximate the same total-volume calculation. If negative flow represents water leaving, its contribution subtracts, so the integral measures net change rather than all water that ever passed the valve.

concepts.title: Gradient
concepts.mechanism: A gradient keeps separate the sensitivities to different adjustable inputs. It answers what would happen if we changed each coordinate while leaving the others fixed. Combining those sensitivities lets an optimization algorithm choose a coordinated step instead of blindly testing every possible change.
concepts.workedSteps: At the displayed point, increasing x by 0.01 alone raises the score by about 0.02; increasing y by 0.01 alone raises it by about 0.12. The y direction is locally more sensitive in these units. A small step opposite both gradient coordinates should lower the score, but the gradient must be recalculated as the point moves.

concepts.title: Hessian and curvature
concepts.mechanism: The gradient gives the current slope; the Hessian describes how that slope changes as we move. Large positive curvature means a narrow, steepening valley, while different signs reveal directions with different behavior. This helps explain why a step size that is comfortable in one direction may overshoot in another.
concepts.workedSteps: The x slope is twice x, and the y slope is six times y. Changing x by one unit therefore changes its slope by 2; changing y by one changes its slope by 6. The zero off-diagonal entries mean those slope changes do not couple the coordinates in this example. The valley is steeper in y even though both directions lead upward from the origin.

concepts.title: Chain rule
concepts.mechanism: A composed calculation can be understood one small operation at a time. First record intermediate values on the way forward, then multiply the sensitivities along each path on the way back. This makes derivatives of a long computation manageable without expanding it into one enormous formula.
concepts.workedSteps: A tiny increase in x is doubled on its way to u. Near the current u, squaring multiplies that small change by about 12, so the full change is amplified by about 24. Omitting either stage would answer a different sensitivity question. When two branches both affect the output, their effects add because both changes reach the same final quantity.

concepts.title: Optimization
concepts.mechanism: An optimization problem needs three ingredients: adjustable choices, a score, and rules describing what choices are allowed. The algorithm searches among those choices; it does not decide whether the chosen score represents the real goal. A model can optimize its stated objective very well while solving the wrong practical problem.
concepts.workedSteps: The score measures squared distance from 3, so without the restriction we would choose 3. The allowed interval ends at 2, making 2 the nearest permitted choice. This separates the best possible score from the best feasible score. Checking constraints after finding an unconstrained answer would miss the actual problem we were asked to solve.

concepts.title: Lagrange multipliers
concepts.mechanism: At a regular constrained optimum, moving along the allowed set cannot improve the objective to first order. The multiplier expresses the balance between the objective's gradient and the constraint's gradient. Solving those equations finds candidates; checking the allowed set and the objective still matters.
concepts.workedSteps: The equality rule leaves only one freedom: increasing x forces y to decrease by the same amount. At the equal split, these opposing first-order effects balance. Here the squared objective rises for every unequal split, so the candidate is the minimum. In a different objective, the same method could instead identify a maximum or another stationary candidate.

concepts.title: Gradient descent
concepts.mechanism: A training loop repeats three actions: evaluate the objective, calculate its current gradient, and update the parameters. The gradient is a local guide, so each step uses newly calculated information. This replaces an exhaustive search through all possible parameter combinations with a sequence of small, informed moves.
concepts.workedSteps: The first step moves toward zero because the slope at 3 is positive. At the new value 2.4 the slope is smaller, so the next step must use that new slope rather than reuse 6. Repetition can approach the bottom of this simple bowl. A step that is too large can cross the bowl and land at a higher loss; decreasing loss is something to check, not assume.

concepts.title: Dataset and features
concepts.mechanism: Before choosing an algorithm, decide what one row represents, which measurements will be available at prediction time, and what answer is wanted. A feature's name, units and ordering are part of that agreement. A target is not an extra input that the model is allowed to look at when predicting.
concepts.workedSteps: If the task is predicting floor area, the known targets for these two rooms are 6 and 12 square metres. The two dimensions form each input; area is the answer used to check a prediction. A future room must use the same column order and units. Replacing width with area in the input would change the task and could accidentally reveal the answer.

concepts.title: Linear regression
concepts.mechanism: The learned line is a compact rule that can be evaluated on a new input without refitting. Its usefulness depends on the relationship staying sufficiently similar to the training data. A straight line is a deliberate restriction: it can capture a trend without reproducing every noisy observation.
concepts.workedSteps: The slope means an additional kilometre adds two dollars to the predicted fare, and the intercept supplies the starting three dollars. Those meanings were inferred jointly from all three trips, not specified by a programmer. Check future trips separately: a line that fits these observations best need not remain accurate for very long journeys or a different pricing system.

concepts.title: Mean squared error
concepts.mechanism: A loss turns a collection of prediction errors into a single score that different parameter settings can be compared against. Squared errors avoid cancellation and make a large miss disproportionately costly. The average makes scores comparable across datasets of different sizes, when the cases and target scales are comparable.
concepts.workedSteps: The first prediction misses by one unit and the second by two. Their squared contributions are 1 and 4, so the second miss contributes four times as much, not twice as much. A training procedure can change the predictions and recompute this score. Minimizing it chooses what “better” means; if large errors should not dominate so strongly, another loss may be more suitable.

concepts.title: Supervised learning
concepts.mechanism: Training needs both a family of candidate rules and an algorithm for choosing among them. The labels supply a correction signal: predict, compare with the known target, and improve the rule across examples. The final test is whether that rule works on cases not used to choose it.
concepts.workedSteps: A rule that simply returns the input misses all three targets. Within the family of straight lines through the origin, doubling the input removes every training error. That is evidence for the rule within this chosen family, not proof that nature must double every future value: many more complicated rules could also fit three points. The prediction at 4 therefore needs a fresh check.

concepts.title: Parameter and hyperparameter
concepts.mechanism: Parameters change inside the training procedure; hyperparameters determine how that procedure runs or which kinds of rule it can consider. Their roles depend on the procedure, not on whether the values happen to be numbers. Hyperparameters are usually compared using validation results, because training fit alone rewards overly flexible choices.
concepts.workedSteps: Training calculates a gradient and uses it to change w; the value 0.01 controls the size of that change. To compare two learning rates, run training separately with each rate and examine validation performance. Editing w directly chooses a model coefficient; editing the learning rate changes the process that will discover coefficients.

concepts.title: Training, validation and test
concepts.mechanism: The separation protects the meaning of an evaluation. Training examples influence fitted weights; validation examples influence choices such as model size or when to stop. Once those choices are fixed, the test set provides a less tailored check. Repeatedly choosing changes because they improve the test score turns that set into another validation set.
concepts.workedSteps: Fit each candidate on the same 70 training wells, then use the 15 validation wells to select a candidate. Only then evaluate once on the remaining 15. The counts alone do not make the design valid: if the intended use is on new wells, measurements from one well should not be scattered across the groups. The split must imitate the future prediction task.

concepts.title: Data leakage
concepts.mechanism: Leakage changes the question an evaluation answers. A model may appear to predict unseen situations while actually using a clue derived from the answer or a near-duplicate training case. Prevent it by defining what information is available at prediction time and enforcing that boundary throughout splitting, preprocessing and fitting.
concepts.workedSteps: The overlapping-window example is a problem when the goal is performance on a new well: the test should not reward recognition of the same measurements. If the goal were predicting a later depth in an already observed well, we would need a different split that respects the order and information available at that time. The correct fix follows the intended use, not a universal random-split recipe.

concepts.title: Normalization
concepts.mechanism: Rescaling changes how numerical differences influence a model. A distance-based method can otherwise treat a large-unit feature as more important just because its numbers are larger. Estimate the reference statistics from training data, then reuse those same statistics on validation, test and future inputs.
concepts.workedSteps: Subtracting 100 gives an excess of 40 in the original units. Dividing by 20 says the new value is two training standard deviations above the training mean. It is not a probability and need not lie between zero and one. A constant feature has zero standard deviation, so it needs a separate handling rule rather than division by zero.

concepts.title: k-nearest neighbors
concepts.mechanism: This method stores examples instead of fitting a single prediction formula. For a new input, compute distances, select the closest k rows, then combine only their target values. The choices of features, scaling and k determine which cases count as relevant evidence.
concepts.workedSteps: Make the neighbor search explicit: suppose the stored input positions are 1, 4 and 7 with the displayed targets 2, 4 and 9. A query at 5 has distances 4, 1 and 2. With three neighbors, all three targets contribute to the prediction 5; with one neighbor, only the target at position 4 contributes. Using more neighbors smooths the prediction, but may blend examples from genuinely different regions.

concepts.title: Decision trees
concepts.mechanism: Training builds the tests from data. A candidate split divides the training rows, assigns a prediction to each resulting group, and is scored by how well those predictions fit. The procedure repeats within groups until a stopping rule is reached. Prediction later just follows the learned tests.
concepts.workedSteps: For a small training set, take inputs 2, 4, 7 and 9 with targets 2, 2, 8 and 8. Before splitting, the mean target is 5 and every row has squared error 9. Splitting at 5 creates two constant-target groups: their means are 2 and 8, with zero training error. This explains how the displayed rule could be learned. With noisy data, continuing to split can memorize accidents rather than useful patterns.

concepts.title: Overfitting
concepts.mechanism: More flexibility usually makes training data easier to fit, including their noise. To distinguish useful learning from memorization, follow performance on data that did not fit the parameters. A widening gap is evidence to investigate, although a changed data distribution can also make test performance worse.

During development, compare candidate complexity or training duration on validation data rather than repeatedly tuning against this test result. A simpler model may make slightly more training errors and fewer new-case errors, which is the useful tradeoff.

concepts.title: Regularization
concepts.mechanism: The penalty changes the training objective, so the optimizer may accept a little more prediction error to avoid an overly sensitive rule. Its strength is a choice that must be checked on validation data. Regularization can help when examples are limited or noisy; an excessively strong penalty can erase a useful relationship.

concepts.title: Random forests
concepts.mechanism: Train separate trees on varied samples and feature choices, then combine their outputs. Randomness helps the trees make different mistakes; averaging can cancel part of that variation. It cannot remove an error that every tree shares, and adding identical trees contributes no new information.
concepts.workedSteps: For the same new input, one tree predicts low, another in the middle and another high. The ensemble's 4 is the average of their outputs, not a new target supplied to training. With a three-row training set, one bootstrap sample could repeat the first row and omit the second; another tree can see a different sample. Those differing training views are one source of prediction diversity.

concepts.title: Gradient boosting
concepts.mechanism: Unlike a forest of separately trained predictors, boosting deliberately makes the next learner depend on the current ensemble's errors. It starts with a simple baseline, fits a correction across many rows, adds a scaled version of it, and repeats. The correction must itself be predictable from the inputs; it is not access to the true target at inference time.

Residuals are 2, 2, −2 and −2. A tree that splits between inputs 2 and 3 can learn those two mean residuals. Adding one-tenth of its output raises predictions in the first region to 4.2 and lowers those in the second to 3.8. At prediction time, evaluate the baseline and the saved correction trees; the targets are no longer needed.

concepts.title: Class imbalance, precision and recall
concepts.mechanism: Choose a positive class that represents the event you want to find. Precision asks whether an alert can be trusted; recall asks how many real events were caught. Changing the score threshold changes which cases become alerts and can trade missed events against false alarms. The useful balance depends on the consequences of each mistake.

These are different denominators and answer different operational questions. A user reviewing alerts cares about the first; a user trying not to miss positives cares about the second. concepts.mechanism: The result also depends on what intervention is being compared, for whom, and over what time period. An average effect can differ across groups. A credible design makes the comparison interpretable; an uncertainty estimate then describes how precisely the available experiment estimates that effect.

concepts.title: Domain shift and adaptation
concepts.mechanism: First identify what changed: the mix of inputs, the measurement process, or the relationship between inputs and answers. These changes call for different responses. Adaptation may correct preprocessing or update fitted parameters using target-site examples, but it should be evaluated on target cases excluded from those updates.

If the physical input-target relationship changed, rescaling alone may not help. Reserve some new-site cases for evaluation, adapt using the others, then compare old and adapted models on the same reserved cases. That tests improvement on the intended setting rather than another source-site score.

concepts.title: Active learning
concepts.mechanism: The learning loop alternates between choosing an unlabeled case, obtaining its real label, and retraining. The label supplies information that the current model lacks; selecting a case is not itself learning its answer. Uncertainty is one useful signal, but repeatedly choosing near-duplicates or corrupted cases can waste the budget.
concepts.workedSteps: The first case is near an even split between the two predicted classes, so its label could resolve an uncertainty. Send that case to a qualified labeler, add the returned answer to training data, and update the model before making the next selection. If all uncertain cases are almost identical, choosing a less uncertain but different case may teach more about another region.

concepts.title: Artificial neuron
concepts.mechanism: The weights say how strongly each input contributes, while the bias shifts the total even when the inputs are zero. The activation then changes that total into the neuron's output. Training learns the weights and bias from errors across examples; the activation rule is chosen as part of the network design.
concepts.workedSteps: The two weighted contributions are 6 and −2. Add them, then the bias, to obtain the pre-activation 5; this activation (called ReLU) keeps it because it is positive. For input values 0 and 2, the same neuron instead totals −3, so ReLU returns zero. One set of learned weights therefore responds differently to different inputs. Linking many such responses lets a network describe more than one straight-line relationship.

concepts.title: Sigmoid
concepts.mechanism: The curved shape turns any real score into a number strictly between zero and one. This is useful for a binary prediction when the model is trained to give that number a probability interpretation. The shape alone does not guarantee accurate probabilities. Its slope also explains why changing a very large positive or negative score has little effect on the output.
concepts.workedSteps: A score of zero sits halfway between the two extremes. Raising it to 2 raises the output substantially, but raising an already large score from 6 to 8 changes it only from about 0.9975 to 0.9997. The output is approaching its upper limit. During training, the derivative measures how strongly an upstream score change reaches the output; it is not another prediction or a second activation.

concepts.title: ReLU
concepts.mechanism: A neuron first forms a weighted sum; ReLU decides which side of zero that sum occupies. Keeping positive values while suppressing negative ones lets a network switch between different linear behaviors. Without nonlinear activations, stacking linear layers would still produce a single linear transformation.
concepts.workedSteps: Move the input from −8 to −7: both outputs stay zero. Move it from 6 to 7: the output rises by one. That change of behavior is the useful nonlinearity. At exactly zero the mathematical derivative is undefined; implementations choose a convention for training. A unit that stays negative on every example can receive no gradient through this gate and stop contributing.

concepts.title: Forward pass
concepts.mechanism: A forward pass evaluates the network with its current parameters. Each layer consumes the preceding layer's output, so intermediate values must be computed in dependency order. During training, compare the final prediction with its target to get a loss. During ordinary prediction, the target and loss are not required.
concepts.workedSteps: The prediction 2 differs from the target 6 by −4, giving squared loss 16. Now keep the same weight but change the input to 3: the prediction becomes 3. This changes an input, not the model. Conversely, changing the weight to 2 would make the original input predict 4, with loss 4. Deciding which weight change helps is the job of backpropagation and optimization, not the forward pass itself.

concepts.title: Backpropagation
concepts.mechanism: Backpropagation reuses the intermediate values from the forward pass and combines local derivatives in reverse order. The result is a gradient for every trainable parameter, not an updated network. An optimizer uses those gradients to change the parameters; another forward pass is needed to measure the resulting error.
concepts.workedSteps: The negative gradient says that increasing the weight slightly should decrease this loss. With learning rate 0.1, subtracting one-tenth of −16 changes the weight from 1 to 2.6. Run forward again: the prediction is 5.2 and squared loss is 0.64. This closes one learning cycle. The gradient described the old weight; further training must recompute it, and a much larger step can overshoot.

concepts.title: Mini-batch gradient descent
concepts.mechanism: Each example proposes a gradient using the same current parameters. Average those proposals before making one shared update. A mini-batch balances the cost of reading all examples against the variability of an update based on only one; hardware can also process its examples together.
concepts.workedSteps: The two examples both push the weight down, with different strengths. Their average 4 gives a single update of −0.4. This is not two consecutive updates: after the first of those, the second example would see a changed weight and usually produce a different gradient. On the next mini-batch, calculate new predictions and gradients using the updated weight 0.6.

concepts.title: Epoch
concepts.mechanism: An epoch describes coverage of the training set, not how much a model has learned. Usually the examples are shuffled between passes, then divided into mini-batches again. The parameters carry forward, so seeing the same example in a later epoch can produce a different prediction and gradient.
concepts.workedSteps: After five batches of 20, all 100 examples have been used once. Start the next pass with the weights resulting from the fifth update, not with the initial weights. Training for more epochs may improve the fit but eventually overfit, so monitor held-out validation performance. If the dataset instead had 103 examples and partial batches were retained, the sixth batch would contain only three.

concepts.title: Deep neural network
concepts.mechanism: A hidden layer is an intermediate representation computed by the network, rather than a target we supplied. Training adjusts all layers so that these intermediate transformations support the final task. Depth composes simple transformations; it does not by itself guarantee better learning.

The gates therefore matter. If both ReLUs were removed, multiplying out the layers would give one straight-line rule, with output −6 at input 0 instead of zero.

concepts.title: Convolutional neural networks
concepts.mechanism: A convolutional layer slides the same learned filter over different locations. Weight sharing lets a pattern detector respond wherever that pattern appears, while using fewer parameters than independent weights at every location. Multiple filters can detect different local patterns; later layers combine their responses.
concepts.workedSteps: The filter compares each value with its right neighbor. Both pairs in the rising signal give −1. A falling pair, such as 3 followed by 1, gives 2, so the sign and size describe the local change. Training can learn these two filter weights from a task loss; they are supplied here only to make the operation visible. The output remains a sequence of local responses, not yet a class label.

concepts.title: Graph neural networks
concepts.mechanism: A graph supplies relationships explicitly through its edges. Each node collects messages from its neighbors, combines them, and updates its own representation. Shared update rules allow the same operation at every node. After another layer, information can arrive from nodes two edges away.
concepts.workedSteps: The neighbors contribute an average of 3, which combines with the node's own 1 to give 4. Compute all nodes' new values from their old values before starting another round; otherwise the result depends on visiting order. In a learned network, trainable transformations can control the messages and updates. This toy rule fixes them so we can see exactly how the connections move information.

concepts.title: Softmax
concepts.mechanism: Softmax compares scores for mutually exclusive alternatives. Increasing one score increases its share and reduces the others' shares; no score is converted independently. Adding the same constant to every score leaves the distribution unchanged because only relative scores matter.
concepts.workedSteps: Exponentiation turns the two scores into positive weights 1 and 3, then division by their total 4 gives the probabilities. The second class receives three times as much probability as the first. These probabilities can supply a prediction, a sampled choice, or a training loss. In code, subtracting the largest score before exponentiation gives the same probabilities while avoiding very large intermediate numbers.

concepts.title: Cross-entropy
concepts.mechanism: For a known correct class, cross-entropy penalizes the probability assigned to that class. It connects a probabilistic prediction to a scalar training objective. Confidently excluding the right answer is penalized much more than making a mildly uncertain prediction, so wrong confidence matters as well as which class was largest.
concepts.workedSteps: Both examples have the same true class; only the model's confidence changes. Moving its probability from 0.1 to 0.9 reduces loss by about 2.198. With several labeled rows, calculate each row's loss and average them before computing the gradient. At inference time, the model still produces probabilities, but this supervised loss cannot be calculated until the true answer is available.

concepts.title: KL divergence
concepts.mechanism: KL divergence compares whole distributions, weighting each log ratio by how often that outcome occurs under the first distribution. Reversing the distributions changes the question and usually changes the result. It is useful for training one distribution to match another, rather than measuring distance between individual samples.
concepts.workedSteps: The first distribution puts all its mass on the first outcome, so only that outcome contributes to this direction of KL. The second distribution wastes half its mass elsewhere, costing about 0.693. Reverse them and the comparison is infinite: the second outcome now has positive reference probability but zero probability under the approximating distribution. This is why order and support matter, not just the numerical difference between probability entries.

concepts.title: Self-supervised learning
concepts.mechanism: Construct a prediction task from the data itself: hide part, transform it, or ask for the next element, and use the withheld information as the target. The model must predict from the permitted view. Repeating this process supplies training examples without a human writing a separate label for every case.

A prediction of 5 is an error, so backpropagation can change the predictor's weights. Repeating across many different sequences can teach useful regularities. concepts.title: Embedding
concepts.mechanism: An embedding table starts with numerical vectors that need not have useful geometry. A learning objective updates them so that their relationships help solve a task. A task that rewards identifying similar contexts could move cat and dog closer together while keeping rock farther away. That would change the table entries themselves. concepts.title: Cosine similarity
concepts.mechanism: Cosine similarity compares direction while ignoring positive changes of length. This can be useful when the pattern across coordinates matters more than overall strength. It also discards magnitude information that could matter for another task, and its meaning depends on the representation being compared.
concepts.workedSteps: The first vector has length 1, the second length 2, and their dot product is 2. Dividing by the product of lengths removes that scale difference, producing similarity 1. Turning the second vector to point the opposite way would give −1; turning it perpendicular would give zero. Neither value by itself tells us whether the underlying items are relevant without a useful embedding.

concepts.title: Contrastive learning
concepts.mechanism: Create two related views of one example, encode them, and score their similarity against alternative examples. The loss rewards selecting the related view. Backpropagation then updates the encoder, so future representations change; the model is learning a geometry rather than memorizing a provided list of similarities.
concepts.workedSteps: For one positive and one negative candidate, take similarity scores ln 4 and zero. Exponentiating gives 4 and 1, so the positive receives probability 0.8 after normalization. Swapping the scores gives probability 0.2 and the larger loss shown above. Training pushes the positive score upward relative to the negative. The choice of related views matters: a transformation that changes the true meaning can teach the wrong invariance.

concepts.title: Principal component analysis
concepts.mechanism: PCA fits its directions to the training data: subtract each feature's mean, form the covariance matrix, and find directions with the largest variance. Projecting onto only a few such directions gives fewer coordinates while retaining as much squared variation as possible. High variance is not necessarily the same as importance for a prediction task.
concepts.workedSteps: Here both feature means are zero. The two coordinates always move together, so averaging their products gives a covariance matrix whose four entries are all 1. Along the shared diagonal, the projection values are about −1.414 and 1.414; along the perpendicular direction both are zero. Keeping one diagonal coordinate therefore loses nothing for these two points. New points off that line would lose their perpendicular component.

concepts.title: Autoencoder
concepts.mechanism:
An autoencoder trains a network to reconstruct its input. An encoder turns the input into a code; a decoder turns that code back into a reconstruction. The original input supplies the target, so no separate class labels are needed.

Restricting the code or the network makes copying harder and encourages it to capture patterns shared across the training data. A bottleneck is a code with fewer coordinates than the input. Here two input numbers must pass through one code number. Both the encoder and decoder weights are learned by reducing reconstruction error across several examples.

The resulting code can provide a compact representation for another task. However, low reconstruction error does not prove that the code has a human-readable meaning, and unrestricted networks can simply learn to copy or memorize. Test reconstruction on inputs excluded from training as well.
concepts.workedSteps:
1. Start with data and a small network. Use four training inputs: (−2, −4), (−1, −2), (1, 2), (2, 4). The second coordinate is twice the first. Can the network learn to preserve that shared structure using one code number?

Use encoder weights e = (1, 0) and decoder weights d = (1, 1). For each input x = (x₁, x₂), compute z = e₁x₁ + e₂x₂, then reconstruct x̂ = (d₁z, d₂z). Here e and d name the two weight vectors; their subscripts identify entries. This tiny network has no bias or nonlinear activation.

2. Measure the initial error. The code is initially just the first coordinate. Input (1, 2) reconstructs as (1, 1). Across the four rows, the first-coordinate errors are zero and the second-coordinate squared errors are 4, 1, 1 and 4. Averaging over all eight coordinates gives MSE = 10/8 = 1.25.

3. Learn from all four inputs. Backpropagation gives weight gradients ∇e L = (−2.5, −5) and ∇d L = (0, −2.5), where L is the mean squared error and each gradient measures sensitivity to its weight vector. For example, the second decoder weight has one contribution per input: code times second-coordinate error gives −4, −1, −1 and −4. Their average is −2.5. The other weight gradients follow the same chain rule. With learning rate 0.04, subtract the scaled gradients to obtain e = (1.1, 0.2) and d = (1, 1.1). Both updates use the old weights. The input (1, 2) now has code 1.5 and reconstruction (1.5, 1.65). The loss across all four inputs falls to 0.465625.

4. Repeat, then test something new. Recompute the gradients after every update. After 40 updates, training MSE is about 0.0000000012. A held-out input (3, 6) reconstructs as approximately (3.00008, 5.99996). The decoder has learned a direction whose second coordinate is about twice its first; that relationship was not fixed in its initial weights.

One number can describe position along this learned line. It cannot preserve every possible two-number input: try (3, 1), which lies off that line, or change the training rows. Different learned weight scales can express the same line, so the code itself has no unique numerical interpretation. The editable calculation below shows the loss falling and compares the input points with their reconstructions.

concepts.title: Latent space and bottleneck
concepts.mechanism: The bottleneck constrains what the decoder receives. Useful compression is possible when several measured coordinates share structure, so fewer underlying quantities can describe their variation. A small representation encourages this, but its size alone does not ensure meaningful or robust features.
concepts.workedSteps: All three pairs lie on the same line: the second number is twice the first. Saving only the first number is enough because the decoder has learned or been given that shared relationship. The pair 2, 5 does not obey it, so the same code reconstructs 2, 4 and loses a difference of 1. The benefit and the limitation both come from deciding which structure the representation preserves.

concepts.title: Bit and byte
concepts.mechanism: Bits count possible distinguishable patterns. Meaning comes from an encoding convention: the same bits might represent a number, a character, or one entry in a codebook. Adding one bit doubles the number of available patterns, rather than adding only one more value.
concepts.workedSteps: With two bits there are four choices, so one of four codebook entries can be stored as a two-bit index. Eight choices require three bits. A byte can therefore hold one of 256 distinct patterns, but it cannot represent every possible real number exactly. Data formats decide how to spend those patterns on range and precision.

concepts.title: Numerical precision
concepts.mechanism: A finite representation must round some values. More precision can reduce rounding error but increases storage or computation costs. Floating-point formats divide their bits between sign, exponent and fraction, so their spacing varies with magnitude; the decimal rounding here is an illustration, not a particular hardware format.
concepts.workedSteps: Storing three rounded copies of 1.234 gives a sum of 3.69, while adding the original values gives 3.702. The small per-value errors have accumulated to 0.012. In a learning system, repeated operations can amplify or cancel such errors. Lower precision is useful when its speed and memory benefits outweigh the effect on the result, which needs to be measured.

concepts.title: Rate-distortion tradeoff
concepts.mechanism: Compression chooses what to discard as well as how many bits to save. Distortion measures the damage using a stated criterion; rate measures storage or communication cost. Changing the tradeoff weight changes which candidate is preferred, so there is no best compression independent of the task and budget.
concepts.workedSteps: The first candidate preserves more detail, but spends 15 extra rate units. At the stated weight those units cost 1.5, outweighing its distortion improvement of 1. If the weight were 0.01 instead, the totals would be 1.2 and 2.05, preferring the first candidate. This comparison exposes the design choice rather than hiding it behind the word “compressed.”

concepts.title: Vector quantization
concepts.mechanism: A codebook is a finite list of representative vectors. Encoding chooses an entry and stores its index; decoding retrieves that entry. To learn a useful codebook, one simple method alternates between assigning training vectors to their nearest entries and moving each entry to the mean of its assigned vectors.
concepts.workedSteps: The chosen entry substitutes 0, 2 for the original 1, 2, losing one unit in the first coordinate. If training vectors 0, 2 and 2, 2 are both assigned to this entry, their mean is 1, 2; moving the entry there reduces their total squared error from 4 to 2. Repeating assignment and averaging can improve the representatives, although initialization can affect the result.

concepts.title: Token and vocabulary
concepts.mechanism: Tokenization defines the units a model receives; the vocabulary assigns them identifiers. The identifier selects a learned embedding, rather than serving as an ordinary numerical measurement. A useful tokenization balances vocabulary size against the length and information content of the resulting sequences.
concepts.workedSteps: Identifier 6 selects the corresponding row 1, 2 from the embedding table. Identifier 7 is not necessarily more similar to it than identifier 2; the learned vectors carry that relationship. Three bits suffice for each fixed-width identifier in an eight-entry vocabulary, but the table, tokenization rules and any framing information must also be stored somewhere.

concepts.title: Vector-quantized autoencoder
concepts.mechanism: The encoder first proposes a continuous code; nearest-entry selection replaces it with a discrete codebook vector, and the decoder reconstructs from that choice. Training must improve the encoder, decoder and codebook together. Quantization prevents a plain derivative through the index choice, so training uses an approximation or a separate update rule.

Moving the proposal slightly within the same selection region leaves that discrete input unchanged. The reconstruction error supplies a training signal for the decoder; the encoder needs the stated gradient approximation, and the codebook needs its own learning signal or averaging update. Only the entry index is needed to represent this selected code once the model and codebook are shared.

concepts.title: Diffusion models
concepts.mechanism: Training corrupts real examples at a chosen noise level and asks a network to predict the added noise, or an equivalent denoising target. The clean example supplies supervision. Generation starts from fresh noise and repeatedly uses the learned predictions in a reverse process; it does not begin with a hidden copy of the desired clean sample.

If a predictor estimated the added noise as 0.5 instead of the actual 1, its squared noise-prediction error would be 0.25. Subtracting the estimated contribution 0.3 and dividing by 0.8 would estimate the clean value as 2.375, not 2. That error trains the predictor. Real generation uses a schedule of many reverse steps because heavily corrupted inputs do not determine one unique clean answer.

concepts.title: Sequence and autocorrelation
concepts.mechanism: Order can contain information that a collection of independent values loses. Autocorrelation looks for repeated or alternating behavior by comparing separated positions. Different lags reveal different patterns; an association across time is not proof that an earlier value causes a later one.
concepts.workedSteps: At lag 1, each neighboring deviation has the opposite sign, producing three negative products. At lag 2, the two available pairs have the same sign, so the numerator is 2 and this estimator gives 0.5. The alternation becomes a positive match after two positions. The values are not exactly −1 and 1 because this finite-sample formula keeps the full-sequence denominator while fewer pairs are available at larger lags.

concepts.title: Positional encoding

concepts.title: Causal mask
concepts.mechanism: The mask enforces which information is available, rather than asking the model to learn not to peek. concepts.mechanism: One block first lets tokens exchange information, then transforms each token's resulting features. Repeating blocks composes these operations. concepts.title: Assay quality control
concepts.mechanism: Different controls answer different questions. A reference checks agreement with a known value, a blank checks unwanted signal, and duplicates check repeatability. Examine them together before treating a batch of measurements as reliable training targets.

concepts.title: Mineral processing and recovery
concepts.mechanism: A mass balance follows total material and contained metal separately. Recovery asks where the feed's metal went; grade asks how concentrated it is within a stream. The balances close both ways: stream masses total 100 t and contained copper totals 2 t.
